title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district responded to the rapid emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The study asks whether teacher attitudes toward AI chatbots vary by grade level taught, subject area, and years of teaching experience, and it also investigates the concerns, benefits, and professional development needs teachers associate with AI use in schools.

The researchers used a mixed-methods design based on a districtwide survey of certificated educators in one large U.S. urban district. The sample included 1,454 completed responses after cleaning. Teachers answered close-ended questions about AI chatbot allowability for several academic tasks (idea generation, editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation), plus open-ended questions about perceived benefits, concerns, and professional learning needs. The study also used logistic regression for quantitative associations and thematic coding for qualitative responses.

Results showed that willingness to allow AI chatbot use decreased as grade level increased, with elementary teachers generally more permissive than middle and high school teachers. More experienced teachers, especially in elementary and high school settings, were generally more restrictive than less experienced teachers. Teachers also distinguished between risks and benefits for themselves versus students: plagiarism and overreliance were seen as especially serious risks for students, while misinformation and insufficient AI knowledge were more salient for teachers. Professional development needs differed by grade level, with elementary and middle school teachers wanting basic AI literacy and high school teachers emphasizing guidance on student use and detecting AI-generated work. Overall, the paper argues for grade-specific and role-specific professional development and policy support for AI integration in K-12 education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional mixed-methods survey study with descriptive statistics, logistic regression, and chi-square analyses, but it is not experimental and cannot support causal claims. The evidence is useful for understanding teacher attitudes and subgroup differences, but it is correlational and based on a single district.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s findings have clear policy and professional-development relevance, but the outcomes are perceptions and intended allowability rather than student achievement or behavior change. The practical impact is important but indirect and of unclear magnitude for learners.

interventions.use_case: Teachers’ perceptions, allowability judgments, concerns, and professional development needs related to generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT for student and teacher academic tasks (idea generation, paper editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation).

finding.finding_summary: This cross-sectional survey of 1,454 teachers found substantial grade-level differences in attitudes toward generative AI adoption and in professional development needs. Teachers in higher grade levels were less willing to allow AI chatbot use, with marginal effects showing decreases in allowability probability of 0.121 for idea generation, 0.117 for paper editing, 0.135 for full-paper writing, 0.125 for concept explanation, and 0.150 for code generation across grade levels. Elementary and middle school teachers prioritized basic AI literacy, while high school teachers more often wanted guidance on managing student AI use and detecting AI-generated work.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses on allowability of AI chatbot uses, reported concerns/benefits, and professional development needs; logistic regression and chi-square tests

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that generative AI chatbots could improve their own work efficiency, especially for lesson planning and information retrieval. In the coded open-ended responses, 21.41% identified preparing lesson plans or materials as a benefit for teachers, and 13.62% identified increased efficiency; 9.13% mentioned information search support. By contrast, only 4.19% believed chatbots would increase students’ efficiency, suggesting the main perceived productivity gains were for educators rather than learners.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses coded for perceived benefits of AI chatbots

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ comments emphasized both potential support for learning and concerns about students’ overreliance, plagiarism, and reduced independent thinking. Overreliance was the most frequently named concern for students (29.52%), and plagiarism/misuse was cited by 26.35% of teachers for student use; this indicates strong perceived risk to critical thinking and authentic writing development. At the same time, some teachers saw AI as useful for idea generation and concept explanation, suggesting a mixed perceived effect on durable skills rather than a simple positive or negative impact.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses coded for concerns and benefits, especially overreliance, plagiarism, and instructional support

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined teacher allowability of AI use for writing-related tasks. Teachers were least willing to allow AI to edit or complete a paper, and allowability declined with grade level; more experienced elementary teachers were also substantially less likely to allow idea generation, paper editing, and full-paper writing (e.g., dy/dx = -0.489, -0.502, and -0.587 respectively, all p<0.001, n=113-115). These results indicate strong resistance to generative AI for student writing support, especially in higher grades and among more experienced teachers.
finding.measure: Logistic regression on teacher allowability judgments for idea generation, paper editing/completion, and full-paper writing
finding.effect_size: dy/dx reported as negative marginal effects; exact standardized effect not reported
finding.confidence_interval: [0.025, 0.975] reported for marginal effects in tables; exact CI values vary by item
